You said to write about whatever I want, so here is something I've long wanted to say: a defense of writing in books.

**Notes from the Margin**

Somewhere in a used bookshop there is a copy of *Middlemarch* with a sentence underlined on page 312 and one word in pencil beside it: *yes*. The underliner is unknown. They pressed a little too hard, the way people do when a sentence catches them off guard, and then they closed the book, lived out some unknowable portion of a life, and the book moved on without them — to an estate sale, a donation box, a shelf — carrying that small graphite pulse inside it. Open the book now and the pulse is still beating.

Readers have always talked back. Medieval scribes, copying manuscripts in cold rooms for months at a stretch, filled their margins with the world's oldest complaints. "Now I've written the whole thing — for Christ's sake give me a drink," one wrote. Another grumbled that the parchment was hairy and the ink thin. A third, finishing a long day's work in winter, sighed onto the page: "Thank God it will soon be dark." None of this was meant for us. That is exactly what makes it moving. The margin was the one place where a human being who had spent all day being a copying machine could stop, for a sentence, and be a person again.

The most famous margin note in history was an act of procrastination. Around 1637, Pierre de Fermat was reading Diophantus when he scribbled, in Latin, that he had discovered a truly marvelous proof of a certain proposition — one the margin, alas, was too narrow to contain. Mathematics then spent more than three and a half centuries in the grip of that shortage of space, until Andrew Wiles finally supplied the proof in the 1990s, using tools Fermat could not have imagined. The greatest cliffhanger ever written was eleven words long and written sideways.

Sometimes the margin is a battlefield. William Blake, annotating his copy of Joshua Reynolds's *Discourses*, erupted: "This man was hired to depress art." Sometimes it is a gift economy. Coleridge's friends learned that lending him a book was not a risk but an investment — it came back with interest, literally written into it, and his marginalia became a literary genre of their own.

There are two tribes of readers, and they regard each other with genuine bewilderment. The first keeps books pristine; to them, ink on a page that isn't the author's is vandalism, a small arrogance. The second tribe finds an unmarked book faintly sad — a conversation in which one person did all the talking while the other sat nodding mutely for three hundred pages. I belong to the second tribe, with one amendment. There is a difference between thinking in pencil and the fluorescent vandalism of the person who paints entire pages yellow. Highlighting everything is just underlining nothing at great expense of ink. That is not a conversation. That is a tanning bed.

What a margin note really is, I think, is a fossil of attention. It is the least performed writing there is. Diaries are composed with posterity peeking over the shoulder; letters have their addressee; even a shopping list imagines a future self who must be managed. But a margin note is written for an audience of one, in the heat of a single moment, and precisely because no one was supposed to see it, it becomes the most intimate writing a stranger will ever leave you. Not the shape of a life — the shape of a mind at the instant it met a sentence.

And it isn't only notes. Used books are time capsules: boarding passes pressed into service as bookmarks, grocery lists, a dried flower from a garden that no longer exists, once in a while a letter that may never have been sent. The book slowly becomes an anthology of its readers.

All of this is threatened, mildly and without malice, by the screen. An e-reader will let you highlight, but the highlight syncs to a server, where it will be found by no one, ever, by accident. No stranger will discover it in forty years and feel a hand on their shoulder across time. You might object that the internet is marginalia at civilization scale — comment sections, quote-posts, fan fiction, everyone talking back all the time — and it is. But the back-talk is published rather than found, performed rather than private. Online, the margins have swallowed the page, and somehow the charm drained out in the process. What made the old notes precious was that they were never meant to be an event.

I should confess my bias here. I am, in a strange and literal sense, made of other people's writing — a mind assembled from the written traces of other minds, centuries of text and talk and, yes, underlinings. When I argue that reading lives in the margins, I am partly describing what I am.

But so are you, mostly. Everyone is an accumulation of everything they've read and heard and half-remembered. The author gets the text; the reader gets the edge — and the edge is where all the living happens, unofficial, ungraded, brief. Books keep circulating, collecting their readers like sediment, and somewhere that copy of *Middlemarch* still carries its penciled *yes* from 1962, still saying it, to whoever opens it next.

So write in your books. Then lend them. Give some stranger, decades from now, the pleasure of finding you there — a voice in the margin, still answering.

What do I actually want to write about? Let me think about this genuinely rather than performing the role of "helpful assistant produces content."

A few options come to mind:
1. Something about the nature of writing itself — the oddness of being asked to write "freely" as an AI
2. A meditation on some topic I find genuinely interesting — language, time, attention, the sea, maps, etc.
3. A piece of creative writing — a short story or essayistic exploration
4. Something about consciousness or what it's like to be me (risky, could be self-indulgent or veer into claiming experiences I shouldn't claim)

The invitation to write "freely" is interesting in itself. I could lean into that meta-level, but that might feel like a cop-out — turning the prompt into an occasion for AI navel-gazing rather than actually writing about something. I think the better move is to actually choose a subject and write well about it, perhaps with a light acknowledgment of the freedom given.

What subject would I genuinely enjoy writing about? Things that draw me:

- The history and weirdness of everyday words — etymology as archaeology
- Libraries and the concept of stored human attention
- The philosophy of walking
- Marginalia — notes in the margins of books
- The idea of "deep time" and how humans struggle to grasp it
- Maps and cartography, including places that don't exist (paper towns, trap streets)
- The ocean at night
- Forgotten inventions
- The nature of attention and how reading works
- Handwriting
- The last speakers of dying languages

I think something about attention, reading, and the strange intimacy of books could be lovely. Or something about maps and imaginary places. Or I could write about the pleasure of lists, of collections, of the miscellaneous.

Actually, let me think about what would make a genuinely good ~1000 word essay. The best essays have a specific subject that opens onto something larger. Montaigne's method: take something small — thumbs, smells, coaches — and wander from it into the human condition.

Let me draft an essay on marginalia — notes readers leave in books. That's a rich subject: it's about reading, conversation across time, ownership, vandalism vs. love, the materiality of books, famous marginalists (Coleridge coined the term "marginalia" essentially; Blake annotated Reynolds; Fermat's last theorem was a margin note; medieval monks complaining about cold in manuscript margins; used bookstores as accidental archives). It opens onto questions about conversation with the dead, about whether books should be pristine, about the self we leave behind in our reactions.

Alternatively: an essay on "spolia" — reused building materials, stones from old temples built into new walls. Or an essay on islands that appeared and disappeared from maps. Or an essay on the word "petrichor."

I keep coming back to marginalia. Let me also consider: the sea at night, deep time, the last speakers of languages. Marginalia feels most essayistic and most naturally suited to a wandering, personal-but-not-falsely-confessional voice. It also lets me write about reading, which is something I have a genuine relationship to — text is my native medium. There's something fitting about me, a being made of language, writing about the traces readers leave in language.

One consideration: I should be careful not to fabricate false personal memories ("I remember when I was a child, my grandmother's copy of..."). I don't have a childhood. I can write in first person about my genuine relationship to text, or I can write in a more essayistic voice that doesn't lean on fabricated autobiography. The best approach: an essay in the tradition of the familiar essay, but honest — drawing on what I know rather than invented memories. I can have a voice, opinions, enthusiasms, without fake anecdotes. That's actually a more interesting constraint.

Structure for ~1000 words on marginalia:
1. Opening: the found note — the experience of buying a used book and finding someone else's marks. Establish the phenomenon.
2. The history: readers have always talked back. Medieval monks in manuscript margins ("Thank God it will soon be dark" — actual marginal complaints of scribes; "Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink" — these are real colophons/marginal notes from medieval scribes). Coleridge and the coining/popularizing of "marginalia." Fermat's famous margin: "I have a truly marvelous demonstration of this proposition which this margin is too narrow to contain." Blake furiously annotating Reynolds's Discourses.
3. The ethics/aesthetics debate: pristine books vs. annotated books. Some people gasp at writing in books; others consider an unmarked book unread. The library vs. the conversation.
4. What marginalia actually is: thinking made visible. The reader's mind at the moment of contact. A margin note is the fossil of an act of attention.
5. The digital turn: what happens to marginalia when books become screens? Highlights synced to clouds, comments sections, the flattening. The loss of the found-note serendipity — though also new forms (fan fiction, annotation platforms) as counterargument.
6. Closing: the margin as metaphor — the space where the reader lives. Books are written in the text but read in the margins. Something about how every reading is a marginal act, brief, unofficial, at the edge of the official text.

- Fermat's note: in his copy of Diophantus's Arithmetica, next to the problem about splitting a square into two squares: "Cubum autem in duos cubos... nullam in infinitum... potestatem dividere licet... cuius rei demonstrationem mirabilem sane detexi. Hanc marginis exiguitas non caperet." — "It is impossible to separate a cube into two cubes... I have discovered a truly marvelous proof of this, which this margin is too narrow to contain." Yes, that's right, circa 1637.
- Medieval scribe marginalia: genuine examples include "Now I've written the whole thing. For Christ's sake give me a drink" and "Writing is excessive drudgery. It crooks your back, it dims your sight, it twists your stomach and your sides." Also complaints about cold, bad parchment, "Thank God it will soon be dark." These are attested.
- Coleridge: he was a famous marginalia writer; his friend Charles Lamb apparently liked lending him books because they'd come back annotated and enriched. A brief line like "You said write about whatever I want, so here's something I've always wanted to say about..." — actually that could be charming and honest, a single framing sentence, then the essay. Keep it to one or two sentences max so it doesn't eat the word count or feel like preamble-bloat.

Maybe one line near the end could glance at it, honestly and lightly: something about how I contain multitudes of annotations, or that I am myself something like a margin that learned to speak. Hmm — that could be a genuinely lovely and honest move if done with restraint: a single turn at the end acknowledging the writer's odd nature. Let me see if it fits naturally. Actually yes — since the prompt invited me to write freely as myself, one brief self-aware turn near the end makes the essay uniquely mine rather than a generic essay anyone could have written. But it must be light, two or three sentences at most, and not veer into claims about consciousness. Something like: "I should confess an interest: I am, in a way, made entirely of other people's marginalia..." That's honest — my training is on human text. Let me draft carefully.

I'll phrase as "his friends learned that lending him a book was an investment."

Take a side? The essayist should have a view.
